thread.title_full: Bison involved in fatal incident at Custer State Park to be relocated, not euthanized

author: beaver state news
title: Bison involved in fatal incident at Custer State Park to be relocated, not euthanized
text:
The bull bison connected to a fatal encounter with a 70-year-old woman at South Dakota’s Custer State Park will not be euthanized and will instead be moved under the care of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Game, Fish, and Parks, according to a June 10 announcement from the agency.
Concern had grown that the animal would be put down following May’s incident involving a Canadian visitor. The decision follows widespread online reaction urging officials to relocate rather than euthanize the bison. Photographer Dave Scragg said he encouraged his followers to contact park and state officials. “Our main goal was to save the animal,” Scragg said.
Chad Kremer, Custer State Park bison herd manager, commented on social media that he has been “the steward and caretaker for this bull’s journey of life thus far.” Kremer added, “As a prey animal, unfortunately, pressure was placed on him that caused him to react, not attack, but he didn’t deserve to be destroyed.”
Rosebud Sioux Tribe Game, Fish, and Parks stated that the bison was “acting in accordance with its wild nature” and explained: “We will honor both our cultural obligation to protect our relative and the need of keeping the public safe.” The tribe also offered condolences to the woman’s family and said relocating the animal would place it in a protected setting away from visitors.
Scragg said he believes public pressure influenced officials’ decision: “When this all started, the word from the top was that putting this animal down was the plan,” he said. “We didn’t accept that, and we made sure our voices were loud enough to reach the people who could actually make a change.” He later called it a “total win for the community and a win for our wildlife.”
Nick Harrington of South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks Department said, “Herd management decisions are made with public safety at the forefront, and we will continue to take necessary action to protect human life.” He added that officials were grateful for Rosebud Sioux Tribe’s willingness to assist with relocating the buffalo.
summary: The bull bison connected to a fatal encounter with a 70-year-old woman at South Dakota’s Custer State Park will not be euthanized and will instead be moved under the care of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Game, Fish, and Parks, according to a June 10 announcement from the agency. The decision follows widespread online reaction urging officials to relocate rather than euthanize the bison.
